messages.content:
I’ve noticed there is a bridge that gaps the psychological and the physiological, the mental and physical suffering. I think this gap is bridged by a spiritual component that resides within us—our soul that is made in the image of God. 

I remember reading The Anzio Beachhead chapter in "Pain: The Science of Suffering" by Patrick Wall, on the complexities of pain. In that chapter, it describes how soldiers' expectations about their future—such as whether they are going home or remaining in a warzone—can significantly impact their experience of pain, including the occurrence of phantom limb syndrome. It briefly explored how these factors interact with the brain's pain processing mechanisms, illustrating the significant role of psychological and environmental contexts in the perception of pain. The medical officer, Harry Beecher, asked every single severely wounded soldier, who could speak, the same question: “Are you in pain? Do you want something for it?” Beecher was shocked when he saw that 70% of them responded ‘no’ to both questions. Beecher later concluded that to be wounded on the Anzio Beachhead battlefield had a positive biological advantage over not being wounded. To be wounded and to reach the hospital at Anzio implied a good chance of evacuation and survival. To remain in the line unwounded implied a serious risk of being killed in the war. It emphasizes that pain is not just a physical sensation but also deeply intertwined with emotional and cognitive aspects, shaping how pain is experienced and managed by individuals.

This lines up with the concepts of empathy and comparative thinking. Central sensitization is a condition where the nervous system goes into a persistent state of high reactivity. This heightened sensitivity can lower the threshold for what causes pain and can cause a more intense and longer-lasting pain experience. It's a common issue in various chronic pain conditions, including headaches/migraines. The addition of stress can alter the body’s hormone levels, which in turn may affect the nervous system. Stress hormones like cortisol can influence pain pathways, potentially leading to increased pain sensitivity. Other factors that could be contributing are psychological and emotional factors, behavioral changes (altered by the chronic pain), and neurological changes—chronic stress might lead to changes in the brain areas that process pain signals, contributing to central sensitization. This can make the brain more likely to interpret various signals as pain and can intensify the pain experience.

Psychological Reframing
Empathy and Comparative Thinking:
Learning about someone else's suffering can trigger a psychological mechanism where you compare your situation to theirs. This can either increase or decrease your perceived pain severity depending on whether you see your own situation as better or worse. This is known as "downward comparison" when you feel your situation is better, which might lead to a feeling of relief or decreased personal pain. The opposite can be true as well, unfortunately. 

Attentional Focus: 
Your focus of attention plays a significant role in how you perceive pain. When you're engrossed in your own pain or problems, they might seem overwhelming. However, shifting your focus to someone else's struggles can sometimes lessen your awareness of your own pain. Understandably, we can’t do this 100% of the time, so shifting our focus to different things can keep the attention off of the perceived physical pain.

Emotional Contagion:
Sometimes, knowing about others' pain can evoke a deep empathetic response, which not only makes you more aware of their pain but can also alter your emotional state. If this shifts you into a more positive emotional state (perhaps through feelings of gratitude or perspective), it might indirectly lessen your pain.


Neurobiological Reframing
Mirror Neurons: 
These neurons in the brain activate both when you perform an action and when you observe the same action performed by another. They are thought to be involved in empathy and understanding others' pain. Observing or imagining another's pain can activate the neural mechanisms related to pain but can also trigger brain areas involved in pain relief, such as those linked to the release of endorphins.

Endorphin Release: 
Endorphins are the body's natural analgesics. They significantly mitigate pain and enhance mood. Activities such as engaging in enjoyable hobbies and regular exercise stimulate endorphin release, providing relief from chronic pain through mechanisms like the "runner's high." Nutritious diets and quality sleep also promote endorphin production, supporting physiological restoration and stress reduction. Positive interpersonal relationships elevate endorphin levels, enhancing emotional well-being and pain resilience. They manage chronic pain through endogenous opioid activation.

Cortical Control: 
The cerebral cortex can exert top-down control over pain signals. Emotional and cognitive processes can modulate pain perception by enhancing or inhibiting the spinal cord and brain's pain-processing pathways.




Outsmarting Pain: Physical CNS Modulation
There are methods that leverage physical and psychological interventions to redefine how the central nervous system processes pain. By engaging in certain behaviors like targeted physical activities, doing volunteer work, and trying out cryotherapy, for example, you can trigger a series of neurobiological responses that not only distract from pain but fundamentally alter its perception which might offer extended periods of relief. 


Examples
Engaging in strenuous physical activities can initiate a series of biochemical responses, primarily the release of endorphins, the body’s natural pain-relieving chemicals. These endorphins bind to receptors in the brain to lessen pain and enhance mood. The physical exertion itself also shifts the CNS’s focus from processing pain signals to managing the demands of the activity, providing a form of distraction and relief. 

Volunteer work can improve psychological and emotional well-being by invoking cognitive and affective processes that divert attention away from pain. This mental engagement leverages the gate control theory of pain, where the brain prioritizes cognitive and emotional stimuli over pain signals, thus reducing the perception of pain. This also incorporates the concept of empathy and comparative thinking. It shifts the focus off of you and thinking about your own pain/suffering which can become overbearing over time. 

Whole-body cryotherapy is something that provides a lot of chronic pain sufferers some relief. It involves exposing the body to extremely cold temperatures, which can induce a rapid decrease in tissue temperature, leading to reduced inflammation and slower nerve signal transmission. This 'thermal shock' can reset pain thresholds, making the body less sensitive to pain. It puts the body through extreme transient shock and acts as a hard reboot to the central nervous system. I’d be interested to see how this would work for you over time. You could also look into investing in a cold plunge tub. They can be expensive but might be worth it if the cryotherapy sessions work. Initially, I imagine the cold shock would make the headaches worse and then possibly provide relief over time. 

The acute shock of the cold forces the body to deprioritize its usual pain pathways, such as those associated with chronic headaches, thus providing relief post-therapy. Although initially uncomfortable, regular sessions can transform this experience into a source of empowerment. Patients often report a sense of mastery over their physical suffering, as they willingly subject themselves to this controlled, acute stressor.


These suggestions are just a starting point—you’ll need to explore and discover what resonates best with you. Each approach has unique benefits, and different combinations might work more effectively for various individuals. Engaging in social activities, such as joining a book club, sports club, art workshop, or Bible study group, can be equally beneficial. Often, breaking away from routines that weigh us down can make a significant difference. It’s  important to recognize potential stress triggers; for instance, work-related stress is common, and you mentioned considering taking some time off. A work sabbatical could be something to explore, temporarily.  



Spiritual component of chronic suffering

Since we are made in God’s image, we can sometimes be heavily influenced and burdened by our environment and also the people in it. We see it expressed through Christ who suffered for our sins but even more so suffered seeing the extent of the sinful nature of His creation. The day Christ died on the cross, he restored hope in humanity where it was seemingly lost, as man began to rely on his own logic and works to find salvation. This is the path of the devil personified. I think more than anything it illustrates how important hope, faith and trust in God is that He didn’t abandon His people that are suffering, whether physically or mentally—though the difference is smaller than we think. 

John 9:1-3:
1 Now as Jesus passed by, He saw a man who was blind from birth.†
2 And His disciples asked Him, saying, “Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?”
3 Jesus answered, “Neither this man nor his parents sinned, but that the works of God should be revealed in him.†

There is a common theme in the Bible that the innocent often suffer, and the guilty are often spared earthly sufferings. This was demonstrated when Jesus healed the paralytic and the blind man. It was also expressed when He didn’t heal the Apostle Thomas. 


Forgive me for saying this—as someone who cannot physically relate to your pain and suffering—but this chronic condition should be viewed in a way as a gift from God. This antithetical logic can only come from the most backwards thinking of man but from God’s perspective, based on Scriptural teachings, He often uses people who are strong in faith to serve as examples for others. I mentioned the paralytic, the blind man, and Apostle Thomas but all of the Apostles (and many others) suffered a martyred death through immense physical and emotional suffering. Some people think John the Apostle had an easy life and death, compared to his brother’s in Christ, because he likely died from natural causes. However, his suffering was no less significant. John's martyrdom was characterized by his spiritual trials and the burden of the revelations he received and recorded in the Book of Revelation. This is where the dance between physical and mental suffering comes into play. There’s a quote by an early church father that said, "If someone accuses you and you endure it in silence, then you have truly become a martyr."
It took me a long time to understand that bridge between mental and physical suffering and how it’s also expressed in our own psychophysiological expression of pain. 


Picking up and carrying the cross is not always expressed physically. Likewise, you enduring the long-standing emotional suffering of your chronic physical pain is an expression of this sentiment. The physical component has affected the mental component and yet you persevere not only in a worldly sense but in a spiritual sense. Your bolstered faith in Christ serves as a reflection and source of inspiration for those around you who may not be as strong in faith as you are. In this sense, it’s the same gift that Apostle Thomas gave to those who knew him or have come to know him through the Scriptures. At the same time, it’s a gift to you from God. It’s his assurance to you that if whenever the passions or tribulations you experience in life steer you off the path at any given moment, the chronic pain serves as an enigmatic mirror placed strategically at the nadir of our internal abyss, serving as God’s failsafe for our own propensity to descend into overwhelming suffering. This “mirror” ensures that even in our darkest moments — when faith dwindles to its feeblest ember — there remains an innate potential for resurgence. The light within us, even when dimmed by trials and tribulations, carries the eternal grace of God.
Though it may not seem this way when you are going through those bouts of physical pain and the mental anguish associated with it, it’s important to remember that this life is short and eternity in Christ has no end. If we have to suffer a little in this life so that we can serve others and furthermore, serve Christ himself, then it’s a martyred life we should strive for. Our earthly presence holds significant value for the spiritual growth of others and God promises to reward us for this sacrifice we make in His name. 


Seeking God amidst trials and suffering
- Psalm 34:18: "The LORD is near to those who have a broken heart, And saves such as have a contrite spirit."
1 Peter 4:12-13: "Beloved, do not think it strange concerning the fiery trial which is to try you, as though some strange thing happened to you; but rejoice to the extent that you partake of Christ’s sufferings, that when His glory is revealed, you may also be glad with exceeding joy."


On the Interplay of Light and Shadow:
Psalm 18:28:
For it is you who light my lamp; the Lord my God lightens my darkness.
James 1:17: Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and comes down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow of turning. 

If God is the unchanging and steadfast “Father of lights” who does not cast shifting shadows, then anchoring one’s faith, hope, and life on Him ensures stability and orientation. When our focus remains on such an unwavering Entity, there’s no room for disorientation or misdirection. 


Martyrdom is not confined to the act of dying for one's faith but includes living in a manner that bears witness to the strength and conviction of that faith. I believe John the Apostle expressed this broader understanding through his spiritual trials and the extreme emotional and psychological impacts of his visions. This form of martyrdom expresses the complexity of our Christian suffering, where the mental and spiritual are intertwined with the physical, each aspect bringing its own form of pain and its own type of courage.


Paul's Suffering in Prison
12 But I want you to know, brethren, that the things which happened to me have actually turned out for the furtherance of the gospel,
13 so that it has become evident to the whole palace guard, and to all the rest, that my chains are in Christ;
14 and most of the brethren in the Lord, having become confident by my chains, are much more bold to speak the word without fear.
15 Some indeed preach Christ even from envy and strife, and some also from goodwill:
16 The former preach Christ from selfish ambition, not sincerely, supposing to add affliction to my chains;
17 but the latter out of love, knowing that I am appointed for the defense of the gospel.
18 What then? Only that in every way, whether in pretense or in truth, Christ is preached; and in this I rejoice, yes, and will rejoice.
19 For I know that this will turn out for my deliverance through your prayer and the supply of the Spirit of Jesus Christ,†
20 according to my earnest expectation and hope that in nothing I shall be ashamed, but with all boldness, as always, so now also Christ will be magnified in my body, whether by life or by death.
21 For to me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain.
22 But if I live on in the flesh, this will mean fruit from my labor; yet what I shall choose I cannot tell.
23 For I am hard-pressed between the two, having a desire to depart and be with Christ, which is far better.
24 Nevertheless to remain in the flesh is more needful for you.
25 And being confident of this, I know that I shall remain and continue with you all for your progress and joy of faith,
26 that your rejoicing for me may be more abundant in Jesus Christ by my coming to you again.


Just as gold is tested and purified in fire, so too is the human soul refined and made luminous in the furnace of life’s trials. As Christ chose the path of self-emptying, He highlighted an essential truth: transformation often demands a shedding of pretense, a confrontation with our vulnerabilities. Our journey in life is reminiscent of a refiner’s fire, wherein suffering acts as the crucible, tempering the soul’s impurities and reshaping its essence until it mirrors Christ. Such a process is not just an ascetic endeavor but an intimate union with God, reflecting the teachings of Christ: “I have been crucified with Christ; it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” The very act of embracing suffering and allowing it to mold one’s spirit is central to the concept of theosis. It provides a nuanced lens to understand Christ’s teaching, emphasizing not just the emulation of His virtues but a profound, inner metamorphosis culminating in divine unity.


Guidance through darkness and the transformative power of suffering
James 1:2-4: "My brethren, count it all joy when you fall into various trials, knowing that the testing of your faith produces patience. But let patience have its perfect work, that you may be perfect and complete, lacking nothing."
Romans 5:3-5: "And not only that, but we also glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces perseverance; and perseverance, character; and character, hope. Now hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts by the Holy Spirit who was given to us."

When humbled and made vulnerable by life’s tribulations, the soul, paradoxically, finds itself on holy ground — a space where profound encounters with God occur. The very fragility of the human condition, in its moments of acute suffering, becomes the thin veil through which the radiant presence of God can be most deeply felt and known. This is the true gift from God. 

Spiritual growth and transformation through divine grace
2 Corinthians 3:18: "But we all, with unveiled face, beholding as in a mirror the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from glory to glory, just as by the Spirit of the Lord."
Ephesians 2:8-10: "For by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works, lest anyone should boast. For we are His workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand that we should walk in them."

[2 Corinthians 3:18 makes a profound statement about sanctification, the process by which believers are gradually made more Christ-like in their character and actions. As we gaze upon the Lord (through worship, prayer, scripture reading, etc.), we’re progressively transformed to resemble Him more and more. The phrase “from glory to glory” emphasizes this ongoing, upward transformational journey.]


Luke 17:20-21
The Coming of the Kingdom
20 Now when He was asked by the Pharisees when the kingdom of God would come, He answered them and said, “The kingdom of God does not come with observation; 21 nor will they say, [a]‘See here!’ or ‘See there!’ For indeed, the kingdom of God is [b]within you.”


In a way, suffering and destruction weave the preparatory threads that foster the unveiling of divine revelation and individual transformation. 
The scriptural delineations, particularly in Luke 17:20-21, establish a conceptual framework where the advent of God’s kingdom is not announced with observable markers, but invisibly instilled within the believers. The imagery of desolation preceding salvation - as the world indulges and remains oblivious to the impending doom, analogous to the days of Noah and Lot, foreshadows a calamitous yet transformative renewal. This intense upheaval, embodying both God’s righteous wrath and the imminent Judgment Day, gestates the emergence of a New Heaven and a New Earth, culminating in a resplendent metamorphosis, where the former self is discarded and a renewed, divine identity births from the ashes of tribulation. The eschatological framework unfolds a path, where through the vivifying flames of trials, believers are not merely observers but active participants in a divine story, steering towards an eternal, unshakable Kingdom.

I’ve mentioned this before but the one thing that’s helped me more than anything when I go through some form of suffering is the Jesus Prayer: “Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me a sinner”

The Pharisee and the Publican
Luke 18:9-14

10 “Two men went up to the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector.

Central sensitization 


So, it’s not a purely psychological or physiological phenomenon, but rather a blend of both.

We all have different thresholds for pain, and certain factors can make some individuals more susceptible. For instance, personality traits and our unique interactions with the world can influence our pain perception. For some people, heightened sensitivity arises from a more responsive nervous system. Lifestyle factors, such as diet, physical activity, stress levels, and even mental health conditions like anxiety and depression, can also modify this sensitivity over time.

A good example is "essential tremors," a benign nervous system condition causing involuntary shaking. The severity can increase under stress, specific dietary triggers, or illness. When a person who has essential tremors experiences anxiety, stress or depression, their hands will shake more aggressively. If they consume certain stimulants such as coffee, their hands will shake more aggressively. So, it’s multi-modal stimulation not just psychological. With headaches, it's trickier because they're not as visibly observable. This means two people with the same condition might show different intensities due to varied sensitivities and other factors that I’ve mentioned. 

Advanced medical imaging, like brain scans, might not always capture the subtle differences in our nervous systems (tests lacking sensitivity score for people with a more sensitive nervous system). It's akin to how some people have more sensitive hearing than others. External factors, such as stress or anxiety, can amplify sound perception, while depression might dampen it. Both physiological and psychological components are at play.

Central sensitization is a core component of heightened pain response, which often leans heavily on the psychological side. This might resonate with both of us given our shared personality traits, such as strategic overthinking, being emotionally attuned, and sometimes excessive worrying. Interestingly, I came across studies that have hinted that these traits may predispose individuals to central sensitization, which is notably more common in women and manifests in idiopathic conditions like IBS and fibromyalgia that are also chronic conditions without an obvious or known underlying cause.

Essentially, pain perception, especially for chronic conditions, is multifaceted. External injuries (such as cuts or bruises) might not faze some people when it comes to pain threshold, but when it comes to persistent ailments like headaches or GI issues, their pain perception could be significantly amplified—based on all the aforementioned factors—namely the physiological effect that psychological stressors play on the body, in terms of amplifying pain perception. 

In response to your second question, our brains continue to process information during sleep. So, if you’ve had a particularly stressful day or week, these factors might carry over and amplify headache intensity, especially if your nervous system is already in a heightened state. Similarly, dietary choices, like having dessert before sleep, might impact you more than others who don’t experience central sensitization. For some people, even minor stressors can have pronounced effects on their nervous system.

The chronic nature of your headaches and variance of pain possibly indicates a complex interplay of factors affecting your pain perception. Given the day-to-day variation in your pain intensity, that might suggest that certain factors might be sensitizing your nervous system on specific days.

I recommend looking over your headache journal to discern patterns or triggers. For instance, if certain foods like sugar or gluten consistently precede a severe headache, dietary adjustments might be in order. Conversely, if heightened pain correlates with stressful or emotional events, it might suggest that psychological factors such as stress, anxiety, or depression are amplifying your nervous system’s sensitivity to pain. 

If you’re like me, there’s a possibility that your nervous system has become overwhelmed by certain stressors related to things that are out of your control or relating to personal relationships or something of that sort. The more complications that pile on, the more amplified the pain sensitivity that we perceive. Being aware of this and possibly letting go of things we can’t control and entrusting these feelings onto God helps relieve us of our tensions. But also acknowledging things that are out of our control and being accepting of it should reduce the sensitivity of the nervous system. As someone who has been trying to do this recently, it’s easier said than done, haha. 

The brain and nervous system, in general, is very complex and science still doesn’t understand most things. Hopefully, this might give you an alternative angle to look at things.

No problem at all. I hope it helps! 

Just to clarify, the studies I've come across suggest that chronic pain with fluctuating intensity often indicates a central sensitization factor, which implies that psychological factors play a big role in pain perceptivity but the physiological factors are very real too and shouldn’t be ignored or undermined. So, I’d say def continue with diet, exercise, supplements and everything else that’s been working. 

For me personally, I’ve been dealing with chronic hip and low back pain from repeating injuries. Swimming has helped a lot and not eating inflammatory foods like sugar or dairy, but I’ve noticed the pain intensity often correlates more with psychological stressors rather than food or exercise triggers. Reading about central sensitization reminded me of a book on pain perception, and things started to click. Not sure if it's the same with chronic headaches, but it's worth exploring.

Absolutely, I agree on the identifying and mitigating part cause it’s not as easy as taking a pill, which makes the process complicated. 
For myself, I've been trying to adopt a more carefree mindset. When a negative thought or news item pops up, I try to actively block it out to prevent spiraling into overthinking. Doesn’t always work but definitely helps. This usually wards off the onset of heightened pain sensitivity from central sensitization. By cutting down on stress, even if only by 30%, it could potentially reduce pain flare-ups. The concept of dealing with stress is like an athlete who lacks natural talent (can’t do anything about it) but makes up for it by optimizing other factors like diet, training, and mental resilience. 

One other thing I’m experimenting with is trying to make an effort to absorb more positivity, something I used to overlook. I try to actively seek it now. When people upset me, I try to first reflect on my own imperfections. It helps me cope when there's a disconnect between our perspectives. We all have those personal and work relationships where communication is difficult with some people. None of this comes naturally for anyone so it boils down to the idea of “taking up the cross” and carrying it knowing that others will be less courteous.  

I've also heard some people enjoy solo trips, like cabin trips for fishing, to clear their heads. While that's not really my style, there are a lot of “outside the box” ways to try to cope with stress and all the other different range of negative emotions that might affect pain perceptivity.

The Japanese saying, "Shikata ga nai," meaning "it cannot be helped," resonates with me. It's a reminder to accept things beyond our control (leave it up to God). For everything else, open communication usually clears the air, and we're both adept at that.

I'll keep you updated if I come up with some other techniques. Our situations are obviously different and chronic headaches are far more complex but maybe it helps a little bit, hopefully! 🙏

First, identify which memo came first and explain your reasoning. Second, at the time I wrote the first memo, I made a specific claim about my own relationship to physical pain and suffering. By the time I wrote the second memo, had anything changed that would contradict that claim? If so, what changed and where exactly in the text does the contradiction appear?
